study.title: Jeremiah 34 - Word of judgment and breaking of covenant
study.overview: Jeremiah 34 gathers two messages linked to a critical moment of Jerusalem, when the city was surrounded by the Babylonian army. In the first, the Lord announces the fall of Jerusalem and the personal destiny of Zedekiah: he will not escape, he will be delivered to the king of Babylon and die in peace, even if he is captive. In the second, the focus goes on to the infidelity of the people and the leaders: they made an alliance to liberate the Hebrew servants, obeyed for a short time, but then turned back and reduced them again to servitude. The chapter shows that disobedience was not only social but also spiritual, because the covenant was broken before the Lord Himself. Therefore the divine judgment intensifies: freedom will be proclaimed for the sword, the plague and the famine, and the Chaldeans will return to destroy the city and the cities of Judah.

outline.title: First message: Zedekiah and the right fall of Jerusalem
outline.explanation: The LORD tells Jeremiah that the city will be delivered to the king of Babylon, who will burn it. Zedekiah will not escape or die by the sword, but will be captured and taken to Babylon; yet a death is promised in peace, with lamentation and funeral honors, during the war surrounding Jerusalem.

outline.title: The covenant to free the servants and the refusal of the people
outline.explanation: In the midst of the siege, Zedekiah and the people made a covenant to proclaim liberty to the Hebrew servants and servants. They came to do this, but then returned back, brought the servants back and subjected them again to slavery.

outline.title: God recalls his covenant and pronounces judgment
outline.explanation: The Lord compares the attitude of the people to the covenant made in the exodus and with the law that sent the Hebrew brother to free after six years of service. As they defiled the name of God and broke the covenant, the Lord declares judgment: the sword, pestilence and famine, and astonishment among the nations.

outline.title: The penalty of breaking the pact and the return of the Babylonians
outline.explanation: Those who passed through the parts of the calf, sealing the alliance, are handed over to the enemies. The judgment reaches princes, priests, eunuchs, the people, and even Zedekiah. The Babylonians, who had departed for a time, will return, will besieg the city, and take it, and burn it, leaving Judah in desolate.

study.context: The chapter is located during the siege of Jerusalem by the army of the king of Babylon, when there were still some fortified cities such as Lachish and Azekah. The text also indicates a time when the Babylonians had moved away for a period, but this retreat did not mean definitive deliverance. The reference to the covenant on the deliverance of servants occurs in Jerusalem and in the house bearing the name of the Lord, showing that the rebellion took place in the context of worship and covenant, not only in civil life.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes God's sovereignty over kings, wars, and human covenants. Zedekiah and Jerusalem do not fall by chance; the word of the Lord is fulfilled accurately. The seriousness of the covenant also appears: to promise freedom in the name of God and then revoke the promise is to deal with the divine name with contempt. Judgment is not only military, but moral and spiritual. At the same time, the text denounces the false security of those who think that he can use religion and the covenant only as long as it suits him. In the Protestant evangelical perspective, the chapter calls God's people to concrete fidelity, especially in dealing with others, because external obedience without perseverance is rebellion against the Lord Himself.

scholarViews.insight: The initial section highlights that the Lord would not free the city, although Zedekiah received the promise to die in peace and be honored by survivors of the siege.
The second message denounces the treacherous conduct of the people, who delivered the servants and then brought them back to bondage, acting unfaithfully before God.
The final prophecy announces that the Chaldeans would return, take the city and burn it, bringing complete desolation to the earth.

questions: What does he judge both the breaking of a social promise and spiritual unfaithfulness in God revealing about God?
In which areas we may be obeying God only for a while, but then turning back when the pressure passes?
How should fidelity to the Lord appear in how we treat people who depend on us?
study.practice: This chapter calls us to examine whether our promises before God are sincere and lasting. A concrete application is to review commitments made at home, in the church and in work, especially when they involve justice, care and freedom for others. We are also invited not to use obedience as a temporary strategy, but as a fruit of real fear to the Lord. Where there is anyone under our responsibility, the biblical way is to act with integrity and constancy, without exploiting the weakness of others.
study.uncertainty: The text provided does not include the remainder of Matthew Henry's comments in later verses, so the synthesis of the interpretive context was built only with the excerpts available. It is also not possible to affirm beyond what the chapter declares that the promise about the death of Zedekiah is fulfilled exactly as described, because the later book itself shows different outcome; here, I have recorded only the internal tension between the passages provided.
